{{short description|Determines the fractional part of Bernoulli numbers}}
In [[number theory]], the '''von Staudt–Clausen theorem''' is a result determining the [[fractional part]] of [[Bernoulli number]]s, found independently by
{{harvs|txt|authorlink=Karl  von Staudt|first=Karl  |last=von Staudt|year=1840}} and {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Thomas Clausen (mathematician)|first=Thomas|last= Clausen|year= 1840}}.

Specifically, if {{mvar|n}} is a positive integer and we add {{math|1=1/''p''}} to the Bernoulli number {{math|1=''B''<sub>2''n''</sub>}} for every [[prime number|prime]] {{mvar|p}} such that {{math|1=''p'' &minus; 1}} divides {{math|1=2''n''}}, then we obtain an integer; that is,

<math> B_{2n} + \sum_{(p-1)|2n} \frac1p \in \Z . </math>

This fact immediately allows us to characterize the denominators of the non-zero Bernoulli numbers {{math|1=''B''<sub>2''n''</sub>}} as the product of all primes {{mvar|p}} such that {{math|1=''p'' &minus; 1}} divides {{math|1=2''n''}}; consequently, the denominators are [[Square-free integer|square-free]] and divisible by 6.

These denominators are 
: 6, 30, 42, 30, 66, 2730, 6, 510, 798, 330, 138, 2730, 6, 870, 14322, 510, 6, 1919190, 6, 13530, ... {{OEIS|A002445}}.

The sequence of integers <math>B_{2n} + \sum_{(p-1)|2n} \frac1p</math> is
: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, -6, 56, -528, 6193, -86579, 1425518, -27298230, ... {{OEIS|A000146}}.

== Proof ==
A proof of the Von Staudt–Clausen theorem follows from an explicit formula for Bernoulli numbers which is:
:<math> B_{2n}=\sum_{j=0}^{2n}{\frac{1}{j+1}}\sum_{m=0}^{j}{(-1)^{m}{j\choose m}m^{2n}} </math>
and as a corollary:
:<math> B_{2n}=\sum_{j=0}^{2n}{\frac{j!}{j+1}}(-1)^jS(2n,j) </math>
where {{math|1=''S''(''n'',''j'')}} are the [[Stirling numbers of the second kind]].

Furthermore the following lemmas are needed:

Let {{mvar|p}} be a prime number; then

'''1'''. If '''{{math|1=''p'' – 1}} divides {{math|1=2''n''}}''', then

: <math> \sum_{m=0}^{p-1}{(-1)^m{p-1\choose m} m^{2n}}\equiv{-1}\pmod p. </math>

'''2'''. If '''{{math|1=''p'' – 1}} does not divide {{math|1=2''n''}}''', then

: <math> \sum_{m=0}^{p-1}{(-1)^m{p-1\choose m} m^{2n}}\equiv0\pmod p. </math>

'''Proof of (1) and (2)''': One has from [[Fermat's little theorem]],

: <math> m^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p} </math> 

for {{math|1=''m'' = 1, 2, ..., ''p'' – 1}}.

If '''{{math|1=''p'' – 1}} divides {{math|1=2''n''}}''', then one has
: <math> m^{2n} \equiv 1 \pmod{p} </math>

for {{math|1=''m'' = 1, 2, ..., ''p'' – 1}}.  Thereafter, one has

: <math> \sum_{m=1}^{p-1} (-1)^m \binom{p-1}{m} m^{2n} \equiv \sum_{m=1}^{p-1} (-1)^m \binom{p-1}{m} \pmod{p},</math>

from which '''(1)''' follows immediately.

If '''{{math|1=''p'' – 1}} does not divide {{math|1=2''n''}}''', then after Fermat's theorem one has

: <math> m^{2n} \equiv m^{2n-(p-1)} \pmod{p}. </math>

If one lets {{math|1=&wp; = &lfloor; 2''n'' / (''p'' – 1) &rfloor;}}, then after iteration one has

: <math> m^{2n} \equiv m^{2n-\wp(p-1)} \pmod{p} </math>

for {{math|1=''m'' = 1, 2, ..., ''p'' – 1}} and {{math|1=0 < 2''n'' – &wp;(''p'' – 1) < ''p'' – 1}}.

Thereafter, one has

: <math> \sum_{m=0}^{p-1} (-1)^m \binom{p-1}{m} m^{2n} \equiv \sum_{m=0}^{p-1} (-1)^m \binom{p-1}{m} m^{2n-\wp(p-1)} \pmod{p}. </math>

Lemma '''(2)''' now follows from the above and the fact that {{math|1=''S''(''n'',''j'') = 0}} for {{math|1=''j'' > ''n''}}.

'''(3)'''. It is easy to deduce that for '''{{math|1=''a'' > 2}} and {{math|1=''b'' > 2}}, {{mvar|ab}} divides {{math|1=(''ab'' – 1)!}}'''.

'''(4). Stirling numbers of the second kind are integers'''.

Now we are ready to prove the theorem.

If {{math|1=''j'' + 1}} is composite and {{math|1=''j'' > 3}}, then from '''(3)''', {{math|1=''j'' + 1}} divides {{math|1=''j''!}}.

For {{math|1=''j'' = 3}},

: <math> \sum_{m=0}^{3} (-1)^m \binom{3}{m} m^{2n} = 3 \cdot 2^{2n} - 3^{2n} - 3 \equiv 0 \pmod{4}. </math>

If {{math|1=''j'' + 1}} is prime, then we use '''(1)''' and '''(2)''', and if {{math|1=''j'' + 1}} is composite, then we use '''(3)''' and '''(4)''' to deduce

:<math> B_{2n} = I_n - \sum_{(p-1)|2n} \frac{1}{p}, </math>

where {{math|1=''I''<sub>''n''</sub>}} is an integer, as desired.<ref>H. Rademacher, Analytic Number Theory, Springer-Verlag, New York, 1973.</ref><ref>T. M. Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory, Springer-Verlag, 1976.</ref>
